subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Panspermia: Life from Space?
description: A quick, practical guide to Panspermia: Life from Space?.

hook.text: Panspermia suggests life didn't start on Earth—it arrived from space, carried by meteorites or comets.

buildup.text: Bacteria can survive extreme radiation, vacuum, and cold. Some endure for years exposed to outer space on the ISS.

discovery.text: Martian meteorites found on Earth show that rocks can travel between planets. Life could hitchhike the same way.

twist.text: Panspermia doesn't solve the origin problem—it just moves it to another world. Life still had to start somewhere.

climax.text: If true, Earth and Mars might share a common ancestor. Life on Mars could be our distant cousin.

punchline.text: Life riding meteorites between planets. It doesn't solve the origin—just relocates it.

quiz.question: What is the main limitation of the panspermia hypothesis?
options: It doesn't explain how life originally started—it just moves the problem elsewhere
No organism can survive the radiation of space travel
Meteorites have never been found traveling between planets

details.summary: Panspermia proposes that life's building blocks — or life itself — could travel between worlds aboard meteorites, comets, or interstellar dust. Material ejected by asteroid impacts can reach other planets, and extremophiles like tardigrades show that organisms could theoretically survive the…
details.whyItMatters: If panspermia is real, life on Earth might have originated elsewhere, and vice versa. Mars and Earth have exchanged millions of tons of rock, making Martian life related to Earth life a genuine scientific possibility.
takeaways: Life or its building blocks may travel between worlds on rocks
Mars and Earth have exchanged rock through impacts
Extremophiles show organisms could survive interplanetary travel

faq.question: Have we found evidence of panspermia?
faq.answer: Not confirmed. The Martian meteorite ALH84001 was controversially claimed to contain fossilized bacteria in 1996, now largely disputed. However, amino acids in meteorites and the survival of tardigrades in space are consistent with the panspermia mechanism.

faq.question: Could life travel between star systems?
faq.answer: Lithopanspermia proposes that rocks ejected from planetary systems could carry life to other stars. The journey would take millions of years, and survival is uncertain. The discovery of the interstellar object 'Oumuamua showed that material does travel between star systems.
